lesson.scope: Explain immune memory and compare antigen delivery approaches.

screens.title: The Big Question
screens.html:
The Big Question

Could we teach the body to fight a disease before it even arrives?

Vaccines don't treat an illness; they prime the immune system. While gene therapy changes the host's blueprint, vaccines use the pathogen's blueprint against itself.

How has biotechnology moved us from using 'weakened viruses' to using 'genetic instructions'?

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Traditional Vaccines

Historically, we relied on the whole pathogen.

Live Attenuated: Pathogens are 'weakened' so they can't cause disease but can still replicate (e.g., MMR).

Inactivated: Pathogens are 'killed' by heat or chemicals (e.g., Polio salk vaccine).

Both methods require culturing massive amounts of dangerous viruses.

screens.title: Evaluating Traditional Vaccines
screens.html:
Evaluating Traditional Vaccines

Live attenuated vaccines are generally safer for immunocompromised patients than inactivated vaccines.

👎​

Why is that?

a) Live attenuated vaccines are safer because they are more natural and the body recognises them faster.

b) Inactivated vaccines contain no living pathogen and cannot replicate, making them safer for those with weak immune systems.

screens.title: Transitioning to Biotech
screens.html:
Transitioning to Biotech

Traditional methods involve risks like reversion to virulence (where a weakened virus mutates back to a dangerous form). Biotechnology allows us to isolate just the antigen—the specific protein that triggers the immune response—removing the need for the whole pathogen.

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Recombinant DNA in Design

We use Recombinant DNA (rDNA) to create 'Subunit Vaccines'.

Instead of the whole virus, we insert the gene for the viral surface protein into a host cell (like yeast). That host cell then pumps out the pure protein, which is harvested and used as the vaccine.

screens.title: Production: Hepatitis B
screens.html:
Production: Hepatitis B

Step 1: Isolation

Isolate the gene for the Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Step 2: Insertion

Insert the gene into a plasmid and then into Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast cells).

Step 3: Harvesting

Yeast cells replicate and produce the HBsAg protein, which is collected and purified.

screens.title: Why Yeast for Hep B?
screens.html:
🔑

Why Yeast for Hep B?

Unlike bacteria, yeast are eukaryotes. This means they have the cellular machinery to 'fold' and 'tag' the viral proteins correctly so they look exactly like they would on the surface of the real Hepatitis B virus.

Key point

Protein folding is critical. If the shape is wrong, the immune system won't recognise the real virus later.

screens.title: Recombinant vs Traditional
screens.html:
Recombinant vs Traditional

Traditional

Risk of infection from residual virus.

Requires high-security labs to grow pathogens.

Complex purification from medium.

Recombinant

Zero risk of infection (no whole virus used).

Production is safer and often faster.

Highly specific immune response.

screens.title: The Next Frontier
screens.html:
The Next Frontier

What if we didn't even provide the protein?

What if we gave your body the code and let your own cells build the vaccine internally?

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

DNA Vaccines

DNA vaccines involve injecting a plasmid directly into muscle tissue.

The muscle cells take up the DNA.

The cells 'read' the instructions and produce the viral protein.

The immune system detects these proteins and builds a memory response.

screens.title: mRNA Technology
screens.html:
🧠

mRNA Technology

mRNA vaccines (like those for COVID-19) take this a step further.

They skip the nucleus entirely. The mRNA is delivered in a Lipid Nanoparticle (a tiny fat bubble). Once inside the cell, ribosomes translate the mRNA directly into the antigen protein.

Remember

mRNA is fragile and short-lived, which is why these vaccines often require cold storage.

screens.title: mRNA Process Flow
screens.html:
mRNA Process Flow

The advantage of mRNA is speed. Once a pathogen is sequenced, an mRNA vaccine can be designed in days.

screens.title: Pathogen Evolution
screens.html:
Pathogen Evolution

Rapid Response

Biotech allow us to pivot quickly. If a virus like Influenza or SARS-CoV-2 mutates, we simply update the genetic sequence in the vaccine design without needing to grow entirely new batches of live virus.

screens.title: HUMAN ENDEAVOUR
screens.html:
HUMAN ENDEAVOUR

Public Health Benefits

Biotech vaccines have transformed global health by:

Eradicating/Reducing Disease: Hepatitis B, HPV, and Meningitis B.

Scalability: Mass production in bioreactors is more efficient than egg-based cultures.

Safety: Lowering the barrier for vaccination for vulnerable populations.

screens.title: The HPV Success Story
screens.html:
🤯

The HPV Success Story

The HPV vaccine in Australia is a prime example of recombinant technology. It uses 'Virus-Like Particles' (VLPs)—empty shells that look like the virus but contain no DNA. This has led to a massive reduction in cervical cancer rates.

Fun fact

Australia is on track to be the first country to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035 due to this vaccine program.

The Recombinant Workflow

Order the steps for creating a recombinant vaccine:

Identify and isolate the viral antigen gene.

Ferment cells and harvest expressed proteins.

Transform host yeast or bacteria cells.

Insert gene into a plasmid vector.

screens.title: Addressing Public Concern
screens.html:
Addressing Public Concern

Despite scientific benefits, public perception varies. Misconceptions about mRNA 'changing your DNA' are common.

Scientific Fact: mRNA does not enter the nucleus and cannot integrate into the human genome. It is naturally degraded by the cell after the protein is made.

screens.title: Future Directions
screens.html:
Future Directions

Research is now focusing on Edible Vaccines. Imagine getting a 'vaccine' by eating a genetically modified banana or potato. This would solve issues of syringe availability and cold-chain storage in developing nations.

screens.title: Critical Evaluation
screens.html:
Critical Evaluation

Some people argue that biotechnology makes vaccines 'unnatural'. Based on what we have covered, how would you argue that recombinant vaccines are actually 'safer' than traditional 'natural' vaccines (like live attenuated ones)?

screens.title: Critical Evaluation
screens.html:
Critical Evaluation

You might have said...

Traditional vaccines use whole pathogens, risking mutation or infection.

Recombinant vaccines use single proteins, preventing disease contraction.

Biotech ensures higher purity and fewer side effects from contaminants.

Lab production is more controlled than using animal tissue or eggs.

✅​

screens.title: Lesson Summary
screens.html:
Lesson Summary

We have moved from whole-pathogen vaccines to precise genetic tools. From the production of Hepatitis B in yeast to the rapid deployment of mRNA, biotechnology has revolutionised how we prevent disease. Next lesson: Cell Replacement Therapy.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain how a vaccine can produce a faster response to later exposure to a pathogen.
steps: The vaccine presents an antigen, or instructions to produce it, which is recognised by the immune system.
Antigen-specific lymphocytes are activated and memory cells can form.
On later exposure, memory cells support a faster and often stronger specific response, reducing disease risk or severity.

bank.q: What is the main aim of vaccination?
o: Establish protective immune memory before later exposure
bank.why: Vaccination stimulates an immune response and memory to support protection on later exposure.

o: Instructions for cells to produce an antigen
A new nucleus for each cell
bank.why: Delivered mRNA is translated into an antigen that can stimulate an immune response.

bank.q: What supports a faster secondary immune response?
bank.why: Memory B and T cells can contribute to a more rapid antigen-specific response after re-exposure.
